In [[probability theory]], the '''law of rare events''' or '''Poisson limit theorem''' states that the [[Poisson distribution]] may be used as an approximation to the [[binomial distribution]], under certain conditions.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Papoulis, Athanasios|author2=Pillai, S. Unnikrishna|authorlink1=Athanasios Papoulis|authorlink2=Unnikrishna Pillai|title=Probability, Random Variables, and Stochastic Processes|edition=4th}}</ref> The theorem was named after [[Siméon Denis Poisson]] (1781&ndash;1840). A generalization of this theorem is [[Le Cam's theorem]].

{{Broader|Poisson distribution#Law of rare events}}

==Theorem==
Let <math>p_n </math> be a sequence of real numbers in <math>[0,1] </math> such that the sequence <math>n p_n </math> converges to a finite limit <math>\lambda </math>. Then:
:<math>\lim_{n\to \infty} {n \choose k} p_n^k (1-p_n)^{n-k} = e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}</math>

==First proof==
Assume <math>\lambda > 0</math> (the case <math>\lambda = 0</math> is easier). Then
: <math>
\begin{align}
\lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}{n \choose k} p_n^k (1-p_n)^{n-k}
&= \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n(n-1)(n-2)\dots(n-k+1)}{k!} \left(\frac{\lambda}{n}(1+o(1))\right)^k \left(1- \frac{\lambda}{n}(1+o(1))\right)^{n-k} \\
&= \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n^k+O\left(n^{k-1}\right)}{k!} \frac{\lambda^k}{n^k} \left(1- \frac{\lambda}{n}(1+o(1))\right)^{n} \left(1- \frac{\lambda}{n}(1+o(1))\right)^{-k}\\
&= \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!} \left(1-\frac{\lambda}{n}(1+o(1))\right)^{n}.
\end{align}
</math>

Since
:<math> \lim_{n\to\infty} \left(1-\frac{\lambda}{n}(1+o(1))\right)^{n} = e^{-\lambda}</math>

this leaves
:<math>{n \choose k}p^k (1-p)^{n-k} \simeq \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}.</math>

===Alternative proof===
Using [[Stirling's approximation]], it can be written:
:<math>
\begin{align}
{n \choose k}p^k (1-p)^{n-k}
&= \frac{n!}{(n-k)!k!} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}
\\ &\simeq \frac{ \sqrt{2\pi n}\left(\frac{n}{e}\right)^n}{ \sqrt{2\pi \left(n-k\right)}\left(\frac{n-k}{e}\right)^{n-k}k!} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}
\\ &= \sqrt{\frac{n}{n-k}}\frac{n^n e^{-k}}{\left(n-k\right)^{n-k}k!}p^k (1-p)^{n-k}.
\end{align}
</math>

Letting <math>n \to \infty</math> and <math>np = \lambda</math>:
:<math>
\begin{align}
{n \choose k}p^k (1-p)^{n-k}
&\simeq \frac{n^n\,p^k (1-p)^{n-k}e^{-k}}{\left(n-k\right)^{n-k}k!}
\\&= \frac{n^n\left(\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^k \left(1-\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{n-k}e^{-k}}{n^{n-k}\left(1-\frac{k}{n}\right)^{n-k}k!} \\&= \frac{\lambda^k \left(1-\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{n-k}e^{-k}}{\left(1-\frac{k}{n}\right)^{n-k}k!}
\\ &\simeq \frac{\lambda^k \left(1-\frac{\lambda}{n}\right)^{n}e^{-k}}{\left(1-\frac{k}{n}\right)^{n}k!} .
\end{align}
</math>

As <math>n \to \infty</math>, <math>\left(1-\frac{x}{n}\right)^n \to e^{-x}</math> so:
:<math>\begin{align}
{n \choose k}p^k (1-p)^{n-k}
&\simeq \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}e^{-k}}{e^{-k}k!}
\\&= \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}
\end{align}</math>

===Ordinary generating functions===
It is also possible to demonstrate the theorem through the use of [[ordinary generating function]]s of the binomial distribution:
:<math>
  G_\operatorname{bin}(x;p,N)
    \equiv \sum_{k=0}^N \left[ \binom{N}{k} p^k (1-p)^{N-k} \right] x^k
    = \Big[ 1 + (x-1)p \Big]^N
</math>

by virtue of the [[binomial theorem]]. Taking the limit <math>N \rightarrow \infty</math> while keeping the product <math>pN\equiv\lambda</math> constant, it can be seen:
:<math>
  \lim_{N\rightarrow\infty} G_\operatorname{bin}(x;p,N)
    = \lim_{N\rightarrow\infty} \left[ 1 + \frac{\lambda(x-1)}{N} \right]^N
    = \mathrm{e}^{\lambda(x-1)}
    = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left[ \frac{\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!} \right] x^k
</math>

which is the OGF for the Poisson distribution. (The second equality holds due to the definition of the [[exponential function]].)
